#1790. Former Geordie Guimaraes taunts Sunderland fans as Arsenal show mark of champions

Bruno Guimarães cupped his ears and had a plastic cup thrown at him as the abuse came down from the stands. Despite the missiles, the Brazilian wore a look that made it clear he was very much enjoying his first goal in an Arsenal shirt.

Mikel Arteta has laid bare his quirky management techniques so his players are ready for any eventuality. Late meals and making the dressing room hotter are among his tricks, although nothing can prepare a player having 40,000 fans calling you a “sad Geordie b------”.

So it was a sweet moment for Guimarães, even more so after coming just after Sunderland had a penalty saved. Just 121 seconds after Enzo Le Fée had his spot kick tipped on to a post by David Raya, Guimarães was rubbing salt into the wound with a stunning long-range strike that went in off the crossbar.

Enzo Le Fée is denied by David Raya from the spot 😳🧤📺 Stream with TNT Sports on HBO Max pic.twitter.com/wnoMCDVh88

Bruno Guimarães silences the Stadium of Light with a BEAUTY 🥵🚀📺 Stream with TNT Sports on HBO Max pic.twitter.com/zQHSSLxC3o

The former Newcastle captain gave the perfect response after being taunted his old rivals. “It was a beautiful goal,” he said. “Everyone knows my past, I had an amazing history at Newcastle. But now I’m trying to create a new history here and I have started on the right foot.”

What an important week it has been for Arsenal, who have shown their squad depth by winning in Napoli then travelling to the Stadium of Light and extending their perfect start to the season to six games.

Other teams with aspirations of the title dropped points earlier in the day, while Arteta could battle to a win with key players brought back into the team and Guimarães coming off the bench at half-time. A trip in the Champions League followed by an away game the following weekend is a barometer of where teams are, and Arsenal have sounded a warning after coming through a bruising encounter.

Régis Le Bris’s team offer a challenge that is impossible to replicate, even by the standards of Arteta’s “sabotage” to make his players uncomfortable. Fans belted out Elvis Presley and 90s anthem Ready To Go just before kick-off. Then there was the aggression that Arsenal players faced. There were complaints of elbows being aimed at Gabriel Magalhães.

Bukayo Saka scored a stoppage-time penalty to seal the win but the evening belonged to Guimarães, the £75m summer signing who has been waiting for this moment to ignite his Arsenal career.

“Everyone knows I had a difficult start through injuries in my short time. But I’m glad to be back and glad to play,” Guimarães said. “I feel very good. It was unbelievable to score a beautiful goal, beautiful moment for me and my family and I am happy.”

These are ominous signs for Arsenal’s title rivals, with Guimarães’s return to fitness adding to the midfield options. Arteta’s changes to his starting line-up restored Riccardo Calafiori and Kai Havertz – two of the in-form players in the Premier League – to the team, rather than squad players being rotated.

And his players stood up to a physical challenge. Brian Brobbey used his frame to back into the Arsenal’s centre-backs, who are unlikely to given such a tough assignment this season aside from facing Erling Haaland.

Guimarães was brought on at half-time along with Jurriën Timber, which was another sign of Arsenal mounting a strong defence of their title. With Arteta’s changes altering the pace of the game, the match turned just before the hour mark. John Brooks saw nothing in the incident that floored Gabriel at a corner, but at the next set-piece penalised Ezri Konsa for wrestling with Dan Ballard, much to Arteta’s fury.

Le Fée had earned a point against Brentford a week earlier with a penalty, but this time his finish was tipped on to the post by David Raya. “We should not talk about the save of the keeper, we should talk about what happened before that,” added Arteta.

“But I loved the save from David, the way the team reacted, the way we go again and we go against everything, but this should never happen, it’s not fair, and I am sad, very sad, in that sense.”

Raya also denied Nordi Mukiele from close range when Granit Xhaka’s expertly taken free-kick found his team-mate in front of goal. Sunderland have their own European campaign starting on Thursday and will start with confidence after pushing the champions all the way.

Brooks awarded a penalty in stoppage-time when Saka was brought down by Reinildo Mandava, who was dismissed. “I’m extremely pleased to win again. We had a really tough week, Chelsea, Napoli, winning there and now against a really tough opponent in a difficult place,” added Arteta.

Bukayo Saka wraps up all three points for Arsenal from the spot 🥶📺 Stream with TNT Sports on HBO Max pic.twitter.com/UrLyrykwlh

Mikel Arteta launched a furious attack on referee John Brooks for awarding a penalty against Arsenal and fears similar decisions will cost his team the Premier League title.

Brooks gave a spot-kick for Ezri Konsa tussling with Dan Ballard, although Arteta accused the Sunderland centre-back of a “judo roll”.

Enzo Le Fée’s penalty was saved by David Raya, with Arsenal winning after goals from Bruno Guimarães and Bukayo Saka.

“In my opinion, that is not acceptable. I watched it 20 times,” said Arteta. “And I cannot find a way to understand how you think to give a penalty in that situation or the way the VAR has to intervene.

“I’m sad that we have to discuss something in such a beautiful game at this level. That has gravity because that changes the course of the season and it can cost you the championship. And at this level, with all the work that we put in, this cannot happen.

“You see, it is a judo roll and it brings the player on the floor. So how can this happen? I cannot find an explanation. That’s why I’m trying to find that.”

The win rounded off a positive week for Arsenal despite Arteta’s fury at the officials.

“I’m extremely pleased to win again. We had a really tough week, Chelsea, Napoli, winning there and now against a really tough opponent in a difficult place. We had really good periods but didn’t score and after that they can suffocate you especially when they decided to be really physical and very direct and we had to overcome a situation that in my opinion was absolutely unacceptable at this level. I’m very worried and very sad because this can never be a penalty ever.

“Are you surprised? Are you surprised? No. OK.

“Ezri does nothing. Just watch it. We have a lot of cameras and VAR, and we have to take responsibility to protect the game. Today the game was unprotected and it could have cost us the game and the momentum which is a really, really serious thing,” he added.

“I’m making it very clear publicly because it’s for the game, it’s not only for Arsenal, this cannot happen at this level. We should not talk about the save of the keeper, we should talk about what happened before that.”

Guimarães’s goal was his first for Arsenal, with Arteta adding: “Beautiful, he came on, the goal, the assist, remarkable. That why we talk about the finishers and making that impact and being able to support and help the team. He was outstanding.”

Three points or not, the Arsenal manager is furious about the penalty that was awarded to Sunderland.

I’m so upset – it’s unacceptable at this level. Unacceptable. This can change the course of a season, of the championship. I’ve seen it 10 times, to make sure, because I saw it live and said ‘It’s not possible at this level it can be a penalty’. Because it’s a judo roll, that’s what it is. It cannot happen.

I’ve been in football for 27 or 28 years - it’s not a penalty in any game, in any league, in any context.

Sunderland are a really, really good team and I don’t want to take any credit away from them. It’s been extremely tough and I’m really happy that we’ve done it.

"It's not a penalty in any case, in any game, in any context, in any league" 😳Mikel Arteta reflects on Arsenal's 2-0 win over Sunderland 👀@jules_breach | 📺 Stream with TNT Sports on HBO Max pic.twitter.com/2BUZILexk3

#SUNARS – 54' The referee's call of penalty to Sunderland for a holding offence by Konsa on Ballard was checked and confirmed by VAR.REF: "He's all over him at the near post facing the wrong way".VAR: "I'm happy that it's a holding offence. The foul is confirmed. Confirming…

I feel very good. It was a beautiful goal and a beautiful moment for me and my family.

It’s a very good place to score! Everyone knows my history at Newcastle; now I’m trying to create more history with Arsenal.

[Is David Raya the best goalkeeper in the world?] Definitely. This guy’s an unbelievable player.

What a goal! And especially the time he scored. Coming to this place is so difficult but we dealt with it very well.

It’s a big moment, especially at 0-0 away from home, and they were on top of us at the time.

"What a goal, and especially the time that he scored" 🙌David Raya and Bruno Guimarães reflect on their win over Sunderland this evening 🤝@jules_breach | 📺 Stream with TNT Sports on HBO Max pic.twitter.com/mozUB0mFd8

Arsenal have won nine Premier League games in a row for the first since the Invincible season of 2003-04.

Three away games for Arsenal this season, three wins and three clean sheets. Nobody does it better. The Arsenal players will sleep well tonight because Sunderland made them work extremely hard for the three points.

The match was decided by a dramatic three-minute period early in the second half. Enzo Le Fee’s penalty was superbly saved by David Raya; then the Arsenal substitute – and former Newcastle captain – Bruno Guimares slammed a spectacular goal.

Bukayo Saka confirmed victory with an injury-time penalty. Arsenal are top of the table with 12 points out of 12; good luck trying to catch them.

90+7 min: Sunderland 0 Arsenal 2 (Saka pen) Bukayo Saka’s penalty goes through the hands of the diving Roefs and into the net. That should be the last kick of the game.

Bukayo Saka wraps up all three points for Arsenal from the spot 🥶📺 Stream with TNT Sports on HBO Max pic.twitter.com/UrLyrykwlh

90+6 min: Sunderland 0 Arsenal 1 Saka is fouled by Reinildo, whose misery is compounded by a second yellow card.

Gabriel and Mukiele are booked for their part in that shoving match.

There’s a bit of pushing and shoving from players on both sides after a foul by Isidor on Guimaraes. Nothing much in it.

Sunderland have six minutes of added time in which to find an equaliser.

Arsenal substitution Mikel Merino for Martin Odegaard, presumably for his height at defensive set-pieces.

Big save from Raya! Xhaka takes a corner on the right, gets it back and curls another wicked ball into the six-yard box. Mukiele stretches to poke it towards goal and Raya paws the ball away. It loops up invitingly in front of goal - but then Raya is fouled by one of the Sunderland players charging desperately towards the ball.

A Sunderland corner loops up in the air and is volleyed acrobatically over the bar by Mukiele. That was a pretty good effort, and it only just cleared the bar.

Double change for Arsenal Eberechi Eze and Martin Zubimendi replace Christos Tzolis and... Declan Rice. He doesn’t look injured so it might just be workload management.

Brobbey pushes Gabriel over off the ball and is booked.

Disallowed goal Odegaard’s beautiful free-kick is headed in emphatically by Timber - but then the flag goes up for offside. Not much in it but the decision has been confirmed.

Sunderland substitution Malick Fofana replaces Thomas Meunier and creates a chance immediately with a thrilling run down the left. There’s an appeal for a penalty and then a close-range backheel from Mukiele that is blocked by Konsa.

Ballard clears off the line! Saka swings the resulting corner to the far post, where Havertz rises imperiously to head past Roefs. Ballard stoops towards his own goal and heads clear superbly. I’m not entirely sure Havertz’s header was on target but Ballard didn’t know that.

Moments later, Guimaraes curls just wide of the far post.

Fine save by Roefs! Arsenal cut Sunderland open on the break. Tzolis flicks a neat pass to Odegaard, who runs at a backpedalling defence and tees up Saka. His right-foot shot is beaten round the post by Roefs.

Eyebrows were raised at the £75m fee for Bruno Guimaraes, especially as he turns 29 in November, but Arsenal were willing to pay so much money because they knew the Brazilian was a sure thing. Only a player with serious experience of the Premier League could come into central midfield, off the bench, in a game like this and completely understand the tempo and flow of the game.

Sunderland substitution Wilson Isidor replaces Nilson Angulo.

Xhaka is booked for a sliding tackle on Guimaraes, though he got the ball and felt it was a clean challenge.

Chance for Arsenal Saka puts Havertz through on goal on the left side of the area. He eschews the shot and instead tries to find Tzolis with a square pass that is cut out by a Sunderland defender. Havertz may have been too selfless there.

Dan Ballard is booked - not sure whether it was a foul or for dissent.

The home fans have been stunned into relative silence by that double whammy. It was a mighty finish from Bruno Guimaraes.

58 min: Sunderland 0 Arsenal 1 (Guimaraes) A hammer blow from the former Newcastle midfielder Bruno Guimaraes! Sunderland looked set to go 1-0 up a moment ago; now they’re 1-0 down. Rice played a square pass to Guimaraes, lurking with intent just outside the D; he got the ball out of his feet and whipped an unstoppable curler into the top corner. What a way - and time, and place - to score your first Arsenal goal.

Bruno Guimarães silences the Stadium of Light with a BEAUTY 🥵🚀📺 Stream with TNT Sports on HBO Max pic.twitter.com/zQHSSLxC3o

55 min: Sunderland 0 Arsenal 0 A fantastic save from David Raya, who springs to his left and touches Enzo Le Fee’s penalty onto the post! Sensational goalkeeping!

Enzo Le Fée is denied by David Raya from the spot 😳🧤📺 Stream with TNT Sports on HBO Max pic.twitter.com/wnoMCDVh88

54 min: Sunderland 0 Arsenal 0 A long throw from the left is claimed by David Raya - but the referee points to the spot after a wrestling manoeuvre by Konsa on Ballard!

Arsenal are furious, and that probably wouldn’t have been given last season, but clubs were told at the start of the season that wrestling would be penalised.

Gabriel goes down holding his jaw and claims he was elbowed by Ballard. VAR aren’t interested and the referee tells an irritated Gabriel to leave the field for one minute.

Konsa makes an important challenge on the relentless Brobbey, as does Gabriel on Le Fee a few seconds later. Sunderland keep pushing and Sadiki rakes a shot over the bar from the edge of the area.

Chance for Sunderland A long throw from the right isn’t cleared by Arsenal, and eventually Meunier hits a snapshot that is kicked away instinctively by David Raya. That’s a pretty good save.

Jurrien Timber and Bruno Guimaraes, who is popular in these parts, replace Ben White and Myles Lewis-Skelly.

Tzolis’s deep cross is headed back into the six-yard box by Saka. Havertz stoops towards the ball but is beaten to it by Xhaka, a crucial bit of defending and the last action of a hard-fought, goalless first half.

Ben White has a groin problem and is going to be replaced by Jurrien Timber, either now or at half-time.

Xhaka’s dangerous corner is punched back to him by Raya. He picks out Le Fee, who drags a shot wide of the near post from 20 yards. Sunderland’s belief is growing.

Angulo goes down in the Arsenal area after a challenge from the side by White. Play continues and Meunier’s speuclative shot deflects behind for a corner.

Sunderland have been terrific in this first half.

Mikel Arteta is booked for encroaching outside his technical area. He responds by sticking his thumb up at the fourth official.

Mikel Arteta receives a yellow card for stepping out of the technical area 😅📺 Stream with TNT Sports on HBO Max pic.twitter.com/xDlnL1B9MY

Arsenal are yet to score from a set piece this season. Their supporters have used that fact as evidence they are not as reliant on corners as their critics say, but the truth is that it will bother Arteta and set-piece coach Nicolas Jover. This is the sort of cagey game in which Arsenal so often made the breakthrough from a set piece last season.

Sunderland break through Mukiele, who charges into space and rifles a low drive that is blocked by Gabriel on the edge of the area.

The resulting corner leads to a brief VAR check for an Arsenal penalty after a bit of a wrestling match between Calafiori and Brobbey. Nothing given.

Good save by Roefs Saka curls a cross towards Havertz, who does well to control it on the chest while facing away from goal. He waits for the ball to bounce and hooks an imaginative shot that is fingertipped over by Roefs. Good save.

Chance for Arsenal Tzolis plays a nice pass down the side of the area for Odegaard. He cuts the ball back to Havertz, who screws a first-time shot over the bar. It was a slightly awkward chance because of the angle of Odegaard’s pass.

Reinildo is booked for a foul on Saka. The home fans are getting annoyed with what they perceive as diving from some of the Arsenal attackers: “Same old Arsenal, always cheating” is the chant of choice just now. Odegaard also went down a moment ago after a foul from Angulo.

Gabriel strides forward from defence and sweeps a left-foot shot from 25 yards. It’s a good effort that fades just wide of the far post with Roefs scrambling across his line.

Sunderland will be really pleased with the first quarter. They’re defending solidly and look a threat on the break, thanks in part to some outstanding hold-up play from Brian Brobbey. Saka’s volley is the only shot on target at either end.

Chance for Sunderland Brobbey does brilliantly to hold the ball and find Le Fee, who is fouled on the left wing by Gabriel. That allows Sunderland to send the centre-backs forward - and one of them, Dan Ballard, almost opens the scoring!

Xhaka curled a sensational ball around the Arsenal defence towards the far post, where the ball bounced up awkwardly and was knocked wide by either Ballard or Mukiele, who flew in at the far post. Ballard would have had an easier chance had Mukiele not got in the way.

Chance for Arsenal Saka mishits a volley straight at Roefs from close range after running onto a penetrative pass from Rice. It wasn’t an easy ball to take on the volley - Rice hit it very firmly - but Saka would usually do better.

The pattern of the game has been established, with Arsenal dominating the ball and Sunderland picking their moments to press and then counter-attack.

Looks like it will be a good battle between Brian Brobbey and Ezri Konsa. Brobbey seems to be attaching himself to Konsa, rather than getting into a scrap with Gabriel.

Sunderland break promisingly down the right. Mukiele drives an angled low cross that only just evades Angulo at the far post.

Calafiori has a shot from 18 yards blocked after a typical run infield from left-back.

Enzo Le Fee tries to score from inside his own half. David Raya was outside the penalty area but Le Fee completely mishit the shot.

Arsenal have started well and are dominating possession. So far it’s all been in front of the Sunderland defence, but you’d expect that to change if they continue to have this much of the ball.

The champions kick off from left to right as we watch.

There’s a pulsating atmosphere at the Stadium of Light - you’d expect nothing less - and the action is about to begin.

Myles Lewis Skelly is the first England teenager to start the first four league games of a season for Arsenal since Tony Adams and David Rocastle in the 1986/87 campaign.

We’re in a congested period right now. We’re playing midweek games as well. We made four changes against Napoli, we make another four for today and we try to keep all the players connected with a high level of confidence, and with the right chemistry in and around the team.

We know how tough Sunderland made it for every opponent here [last season] and we know the beautiful atmosphere that they create, the organisation that they have and the individuals that they have. We’ll try to impose ourselves like we always do and come here and be as dominant as we’ve been and then be ready to win the game.

Arsenal’s biggest rivals are still waiting for their first win - and their first goal - of the Premier League season. Alex Connor has reaction to their 0-0 draw at home to Everton.

"For sure we can improve, and we will" 😅Mikel Arteta on Arsenal's strong start to the season 🗣️📺 Stream with TNT Sports on HBO Max pic.twitter.com/nDpwooZq4Y

Arsenal keeper David Raya has conceded only one goal in five matches this season, but he was beaten twice on this ground last season during a thrilling 2-2 draw.

When will Martin Zubimendi start again for Arsenal? Mikel Arteta wants to avoid a repeat of last season, when Zubimendi played more games than anyone in Europe, but it is curious that the Spaniard has not yet started a single match of this campaign. It is one thing to reduce his minutes, and another to turn him into a permanent substitute.

Zubimendi has looked quite good off the bench in recent games but has been behind Myles Lewis-Skelly and Mikel Merino in the battle to partner Declan Rice from the start. And that’s before Bruno Guimaraes, the new £75m signing, reaches full fitness.

In the thick Naples air in midweek, Declan Rice did what he always does: he kept running. Another start for the Arsenal midfielder, another 90 minutes completed and another performance of constructive passing and destructive defending. For anyone who was worried about Rice’s physical condition, it was an emphatic response.

After that Champions League victory over Napoli, Rice insisted he was ready for another marathon campaign. He made 69 appearances for club and country last season, up from 60 the previous term, and believes that is a sustainable number of games, even for an all-action midfielder such as himself. “I have shown I can do it,” he said.

The key question, though, is not whether Rice can do it, but whether he should do it. There is no doubt that his body eventually began to pay the price for his exertions last year, especially during the World Cup, and it would be reasonable for his managers to worry that his extraordinary workload might one day take a serious toll. This, after all, is a footballer who managed nerve pain in his hamstring throughout the second half of last season.

Regis Le Bris, who made 11 changes for the League Cup win over Hull in midweek, reverts to the starting XI that drew at Brentford seven days ago.

RLB's XI to take on Arsenal! ❤️👊#SUNARS pic.twitter.com/F1nXWky4Fp

Mikel Arteta has made four changes to the Arsenal team that won in Napoli during the week. Kai Havertz’s return is the headline news in Arteta’s selection, with in-form left-back Riccardo Calafiori also returning. Myles Lewis-Skelly returns to the midfield and Christos Tzolis starts.

🟡 𝗧𝗘𝗔𝗠𝙉𝙀𝙒𝙎 🔵 Your Saturday night Gunners ❤️‍🔥🤝 Presented by @deel

Hello and welcome to live, minute-by-minute coverage of Sunderland v Arsenal at the Stadium of Light. Sunderland are the latest team tasked with stopping Arsenal, who have begun their title defence in formidable style: they’ve won out of three, including a dominant comeback victory against Chelsea last weekend, and look well equipped to become the first Arsenal team to retain the title since the mid-1930s.

There’s a long way to go, and Arsenal fans will remember how blisteringly they started their last two title defences in 2002-03 and 2004-05, only to ultimately fall short. But right now, they could barely be in better shape. Their fine start to the season came with a Champions League win in Naples, achieved despite a delay to their flight from London.

“I love those challenges,” said Mikel Arteta. “I try to create them in pre-seasons so when they happen, we already experience them and we already know. So get to the stadium very late, change the routine and suddenly the players have to do something else.

“Because when it happens, and it can happen, you can miss the flight, the train can be delayed, there’s so much traffic and I don’t want the players, but not only the players, the staff as well, panicking. So when that happens, adapt to it.”

Arteta has tested his squad in a variety of ways. “[We have] delayed the meals, delayed the transport, taken a different route. We’ve done many things – made the dressing room hotter, more difficult, more challenging, less beds... because we’re going to have to adapt to different contexts.”

So far, they’re adapting very well to the context of being the reigning champions.

#1789. Liverpool: Trey Nyoni impact under Andoni Iraola cannot be ignored

By Axel Clody | 09 Nov 2026 09:57

In a transfer market that moves as many millions as the Premier League’s, where all 20 clubs are looking to invest in signings that can raise the level of their squads, the answer is often already within the club. One such case is Liverpool’s.

Trey Nyoni’s performances so far, a midfielder of just 19, show that the youngster could be the solution for the starting XI until the end of the season. With maturity above the average, the Englishman shows excellent vision, courage on the ball and quality in building play.

Against Arsenal earlier this month, in the Premier League, he led the match in accurate passes (53), pass accuracy (96%) and line-breaking passes (14), according to Opta data.

Against Fenerbahce last Wednesday, he then scored his first goal for Liverpool in a secure performance in midfield. The numbers with and without the ball also caught the eye.

Accurate passes: 89/96 (93%) Passes in the opposition half: 58/64 (91%) Passes in own half: 31/32 (97%) Long balls: 4/5 (80%) Tackles: 2/2 Interceptions: 3 Ball recoveries: 9 Ground duels: 2/4 Blocked shots: 1

In a midfield that is falling short, Nyoni is the positive news that could change Liverpool’s outlook.

That was Nyoni’s 12th game for Liverpool at the start of this season, half of them as a starter. The youngster was discovered in 2023, when he stood out for Leicester City’s Under-18s at just 15 years old.

His prominence in Liverpool’s youth system soon caught the attention of then manager Jurgen Klopp. At 16, he made his debut for Liverpool at Anfield, in an FA Cup match. Before the youngster replaced Harvey Elliott, Klopp and Nyoni looked at each other and smiled together, perhaps both already knowing the future in store for the gem.

In the last transfer window, Liverpool turned down a £30m proposal from Nottingham Forest because they believe in the talent and future of their prospect. So far, that faith looks justified.

The club and the player are in advanced talks over a new contract. The board understand that the midfielder, like winger Rio Ngumoha, is one of two gems with an enormous future who can put their names in the history of the club.

The good news for Nyoni is also that the opportunities he has received from Iraola can be seen more as a belief that he will be a starter for a long time than as a rotation strategy, merely offering a few minutes to a young reserve.

At Bournemouth, Iraola led a talented team of players under 23, with names such as Rayan and Eli Junior Kroupi, among others. He not only managed them, but developed the prospects, raising the talent of each one.

In a season in which Liverpool have many question marks and few answers, Nyoni looks a success. There is still plenty of room for improvement for the gem, but the future, and the present itself, are promising.

#1788. Fridges and pigs and scoring goals

We live in strange times. Sorry to start your day with this shocking revelation, I realise this is a bit of a bolt from the blue, but it’s fact. All across Europe supermarket fridges are being hacked. What a time to be alive. They used to hack, I dunno, mainframes and banks and shit, but now they’re hacking fridges.

Maybe they just got bored taking billions of made-up money from CryptoSloth and BitWomble and needed a challenge. I feel like fridges ought to be the kind of thing you just can’t hack – beyond unplugging it – but what do I know? Anyway, it’s an example of how the inter-connectivity that brings us all together every day is being weaponised and now the sliced meats in your local store are gone off because Neo pwned some large cold cupboards. As if we don’t have enough to deal with.

Such as all the people who hate the way Arsenal play. Let me be very clear, my days of caring what other people think about this football club, or pretty much anything else that’s important to me, are gone. It’s a waste of time. It’s a bit like quote that’s often attributed to George Bernard Shaw, which says ‘Never wrestle with pigs. You both get dirty and the pig likes it.’

I don’t think he actually said that, but I think we can all connect with the meaning. It applies so much to social media, and to many of the ways we’re exposed to punditry and ‘expert’ analysis in football these days. Like one of those shows where you have a couple of ex-pro pigs bleating on about this and that, and then a collection of other little pigs who support all the clubs argue with them and amongst themselves, and it’s just a pigstravaganza of pointless, inane bollocks but it does #numbers on socials so is seen as valuable #content.

I understand why opposition fans go on and on about how much they hate how Arsenal play. It’s because we win a lot of games. That’s the thing that really irks them. That’s just so basic though, you can’t appear to be clever and an aficionado of the game if you just say ‘I don’t like it when they win’, so it’s dressed up as dismissal of style or something else.

And look, here’s where the strange world we live in comes back into focus. You can, and really should, be able to hold more than one thought in your brain – about football or anything else – that holds true. I absolutely love how good we are defensively. LOVE IT. The commitment with which we are determined not to give the opposition anything is truly something to relish. Players laser-focused on their one on ones; putting bodies on the line to block shots and crosses; 11 players moving like a murmuration of birds because they’re so well drilled and organised; off the awareness and discipline; brilliantly timed tackles and headers and clearances; lads sticking up for each other when the opposition get a bit snide, as we saw on Sunday with Jurrien Timber and Noni Madueke refusing to allow their captain to be treated that way; it’s all part of a brilliantly defiant defensive attitude that runs right through this team.

Creating that is not easy. As Arsenal fans we have endured defences that were porous and feeble and, at times, very, very stupid. I do not long for a return to those times. Over the years Mikel Arteta has assembled a collection of players who cannot wait to go out there and do the dirty work of defending, and it runs from front to back because that’s what he demands. If it was that easy, everyone would do it, so to castigate a team’s brilliance in one department because you just lost to them without a shot on target just comes across as sour grapes.

Here’s the other thought though. I’d really like us to be a bit better from an attacking perspective, and when I look at this team and what it’s capable of, there’s no question the forward line remains the area where you can see the room for improvement. We defend as well as we do because, more often than you or I might like, we have to – because we live through games of fine margins. A 1-0 to the Arsenal is part of our history, hard-wired into our supporter DNA (particularly if you’re of a particular vintage), but I can’t lie and wish there weren’t a few more 3-0s to the Arsenal.

I’m absolutely certain Mikel Arteta would like that too, and I think it’s a bit too easy to say that this is a team that plays precisely the football he wants it to play. He is, as we all understand, an arch pragmatist, so what we get is a team that leans into its strengths, as laid out above. He is characterised as a defensive coach, which I get, but a few seasons ago we found an attacking cocktail that drove a title challenge, and saw us score more goals that year than the Invincibles did when they won the league in 2004 (91 to 73).

I think he wants both. He wants that parsimony at the back and the firepower up front. Unfortunately, forward line recruitment is the most difficult part of transfer business, and while he as manager has a part to play in that, as a club our track record is quite poor in that regard. This summer’s window was a complete bust from an attacking perspective, not a good look when you’re pursuing players like Morgan Rogers, Vinicius Junior and Julian Alvarez. When you then let three forwards go and add just one, there are questions to be asked of the people in charge. Arteta among them, of course, but he’s not the one whose job it is to get the deals done.

It’s why there are so many conversations around January, and what we might do. We see other clubs recruit forwards who produce on a consistent basis, while ours too often struggle to find that end product. Is it our system? Would these players find it hard to get those goals for us? Reasonable questions, but the bottom line in my opinion is that we have A+ options at the back and in midfield, while in that front three we’re a bit C-. That’s where the room for improvement is, that’s where the recruitment needs to be better (certainly better than no recruitment at all), and that’s how the games we currently win by a single goal margin, often by virtue of our defensive strength, become a bit more routine.

Simplistic? Yes. Easier said than done? Quite probably. But necessary? Absolutely. Until then though, expect more defensive masterclasses, more pig wrestling, and perhaps someone could hack our own Swedish fridge into scoring a few more goals. Worth a try!

Right, I’ll leave it there for now. I just have a small favour to ask. Arseblog has been nominated for Best Fan Media (Fran Merida) in the 2026 FSA Awards. We’re trying to retain our title, so if you could take a moment to give us a vote that would be much appreciated. You can do that here – https://www.surveymonkey.com/r/fsa-awards-2026

#1786. Wrexham's Hollywood owners Ryan Reynolds and Rob McElhenney jet in to watch clash with Wolves after surprise exit of club's CEO - and catch up with poppy-protest footballer James McClean in the stands

By BEN WILLCOCKS, ASSISTANT SPORTS EDITOR

Published: 08:39 EST, 7 November 2026 | Updated: 10:40 EST, 7 November 2026

Wrexham's celebrity owners Ryan Reynolds and Rob McElhenney have travelled to watch their side's Championship clash with Wolves less than a day after announcing chief executive Michael Williamson's surprise departure.

Reynolds and McElhenney announced in a joint statement on Friday that Williamson was leaving the club after two years at the Racecourse Ground, with club director Shaun Harvey set to take the reins as acting CEO while they seek a successor.

'We thank Michael Williamson for his two years at Wrexham and for his work taking the club from League 1 to the Championship,' the Hollywood actors' statement read.

'Since our takeover five years ago, Wrexham have had historic success on the pitch and won hearts all over the globe.

'We remain focused on our most important task: to make the Wrexham community proud.

'Shaun Harvey has been an integral part of this journey from the beginning, and we know Shaun will give every support to (manager) Phil Parkinson and the lads on the pitch while keeping the broader Wrexham community roaring us on.'

Rob McElhenney and Ryan Reynolds pictured watching Wrexham take on Wolves on Saturday

The American actor takes photos with supporters as he arrives at the Racecourse Ground

Williamson arrived at Wrexham in 2024 and oversaw a period that saw the club win promotion from League One to the Championship and consolidate themselves in the second tier, narrowly missing out on the playoffs with a seventh-place finish.

Wrexham's form this campaign has been less fruitful, with just four wins so far leaving Parkinson's side in 17th place heading into Saturday's clash with Wolves.

After arriving and meeting fans outside the stadium, Reynolds and McElhenney took their place in the Racecourse Ground stands hoping to watch their Wrexham side earn back-to-back wins for the first time this season.

Wolves, who were relegated from the Premier League last season, took the lead in the 25th minute before Wrexham's Lewis O'Brien equalised moments later, to the delight of the celebrity owners.

As the matched ebbed and flowed, both sides fought hard for a winning goal but ended up settling for a share of the spoils, the 1-1 draw moving Wrexham to 15th and Wolves to third in the Championship.

After the match, Parkinson backed Harvey to adapt seamlessly to his new temporary CEO role, saying:  'Ryan spoke to me yesterday morning to let me know the news. I had a brief chat with Shaun this morning; he has been an important figure. He understands everything about the club.'

While watching the 1-1 draw, Reynolds was pictured chatting to former Wrexham star James McClean, who left the Racecourse Ground to join his hometown team Derry City in January.

McClean's appearance at Wrexham is particularly poignant on Remembrance Weekend, given the controversy he courted throughout his career by refusing to wear football shirts featuring a poppy.

Reynolds pictured chatting to former Wrexham footballer James McClean in the stands

Wrexham players, displaying poppies, observe a minute of silence on Remembrance weekend

Clubs across English football will observe a period of silence before matches this weekend, with players also wearing poppy-adorned shirts to honour those who lost their lives in conflict.

McClean's objection to wearing a poppy is rooted in his upbringing in Derry, having grown up on the Creggan estate, where six of the 13 civilians shot dead by British soldiers on Bloody Sunday in 1972 were from.

#1785. Saliba returns with scope for rotation against Slavia Prague

Arsenal are in Champions League action this evening, away to Slavia Prague. There was a big boost ahead of the game with the return of William Saliba to full training, and the Frenchman is with the squad for the game this evening. Whether he starts or not is another question, but he’s clearly in good enough shape to be in contention for some minutes, and that can only be a good thing.

It was obviously a topic of conversation at the manager’s pre-game press conference yesterday evening, and provided an update on how the recovery has gone:

He’s in a really good place. I think the process and the timings and in the manner the injury has been dealt with, and especially the feelings that Willy has been having along the way, they’ve been very, very positive. So, his evolution has been as expected, which is not always the case. He feels very comfortable. He played 45 minutes behind closed doors last week and he feels ready to go. So whether we use him or not now is a matter of what the team needs.

There have rightfully been plenty of plaudits for Ezri Konsa since his arrival, and the way he’s slotted into the team, and there was a question about how he solves the two into three ‘problem’ when choosing his central defenders going forward:

So far we haven’t had that luxury, I wouldn’t call it a problem! We can talk about problems that are very different to that one. The moment that they are fit and available, we’re going to have the opportunity to give players rest or to load the players and to manage the congestion of the players in a much better way than we’ve actually done.

That is most definitely the kind of problem any manager would like to have. There’s no need to rush Saliba back, we can be cautious with his reintegration, and then when we have the problem of deciding who plays in which game, it feels very much like the kind of bridge we can cross when we come to it. But it’s a very nice bridge.

Beyond that, I think there’s some real room for rotation this evening. Players like Ben White, Cristhian Mosquera and Piero Hincapie will be looking for minutes at the back, and if we don’t see either Declan Rice or Martin Odegaard in the starting line-up this evening, I’d be absolutely fine with that. The manager can choose two World Cup winners in midfield, and still leave out one of Myles Lewis-Skelly or Bruno Guimaraes if he does that – it’s the kind of ‘luxury’ he needs to lean into.

Speaking about Mikel Merino and Martin Zubimendi, he said of their involvement so far this season:

They are playing a pivotal role. If we focus on the players that are starting, obviously that’s something else. Mikel has started some games already, some important games and he’s coming from a World Cup, a very successful World Cup. We know the value of the players that we have in the squad. They need to feel important. I do think that they feel very important and we have to make sure that they continue like that because if they have that spirit and that belief within themselves every time they play, they will make things happen for the team to win the game.

Up front, it’s a little trickier. Eberechi was a doubt for the game against Liverpool, while Christos Tzolis player almost the full 90 after his return from injury. I wonder is there any scope to start Max Dowman on the right, which means you can time-share the left between the two I just mentioned and/or Noni Madueke. I think you also have to look at this as another chance for Viktor Gyokeres who did get on the scoresheet against Fleetwood, but on a night when any kind of confidence boost that might have provided was offset by the fact we lost to lower league opposition. His minutes have been a bit scarce so far this season, but you’d be very hard pressed to argue that when he has played he’s done enough to give the manager much to think about. He could really use goals and a decent performance this evening.

I suppose that defeat to Fleetwood might give Arteta some pause for thought when it comes to how much he might rotate, but if you can’t give players minutes in games like this, then they’re not going to be in the kind of shape you need them be in if and when they’re required for more challenging fixtures. It’s not to take anything for granted against a side who are top of their domestic league, but in Europe this season they’ve been a bit poor, and if this isn’t the time to test our squad depth, I don’t know what is. Let’s see!

Before we go today, Andrew Allen has a feature in his weekly Patreon newsletter which covers match day recommendations. It started with restaurants/bars etc close to the ground, but has expanded over time into something much more global. With the help of @bootifulgame.bsky.social – they’ve built a really cool interactive tool which you can check out here – https://matchday.arseblog.com/ – and which now exists as a permanent feature on this site.

We often get questions about ‘Where can I watch with Arsenal fans when I’m in X city’ etc, and there are already lots of places listed around the world. If you want to add to the map, you can submit a recommendation to show where your local bar or venue is, and if you’re travelling somewhere, this is the perfect reference for when there’s an Arsenal game on and you want to hang out with fellow fans. #1784. Tactics Column: High alert at the back stick

A long overdue win at Anfield was marked by a goal, a number of other Arsenal chances, and what will go down as a famous clean sheet, all involving how the two teams defend at the back post.

There were plenty of other interesting things to note on Sunday – Martin Odegaard’s role drifting across the pitch early on and Arsenal’s 20-odd minute spell of dominance midway through the second half both caught the eye – but in the latest instalment of our video series Between The Lines, I look into how Arsenal had great joy attacking the back post, and why Liverpool were never going to have the same luck at the other end.

With the hosts’ defence getting narrow in their own box, Arsenal created plenty of opportunities by having the man on the far side outside that defensive block. That’s how Kai Havertz scored, it’s how he nearly tapped in from Bruno Guimaraes’ effort that flew just wide, and it’s how Noni Madueke nearly teed Havertz up with another tap-in. It’s also where Christos Tzolis was positioned as he came onto a Madueke cross and forced Alisson into the game’s standout save.

Arsenal, though, have no such weakness: their combination of organisation, hunger, and (perhaps most importantly) focus meant Liverpool were never likely to find a spare man at the back post.

The thing squad assembled last summer by Gerry Cardinale, Amorim and the management features a strong starting eleven that can compete with anyone (as was the case in the derby), but at the same time lacks alternatives.

#1781. Slavia Prague 1-2 Arsenal: Slight concerns but another away day win

Arsenal secured another away win last night, this time in the Champions League beating Slavia Prague 2-1 thanks to goals from Noni Madueke and Viktor Gyokeres.

Mikel Arteta rotated in some areas, with starts for Ben White, Piero Hincapie, Martin Zubimendi, Mikel Merino and Eberechi Eze, but relied too on the foundational stability of Declan Rice with Ezri Konsa and Gabriel behind him. We began in lively fashion, and took an early lead.

David Raya played it long, Gyokeres held it up well and hooked the ball forward, and Madueke’s pace took him beyond the defender and into the box before finishing between the keeper’s legs. Solid play from two players who can sometimes be guilty of fluffing their lines when it comes to those key actions. This time they were spot on.

We had more chances to score. Eze showed nice skills in the box but saw his shot blocked; Gyokeres headed back across goal for Merino but he headed over; the Spaniard saw a shot from distance tipped over, and his smart near post run and a right-footed shot from a Ben White cutback forced the keeper into another decent stop; and there was a brilliant counter and pass from Rice that drifted all the way to the back post without any Arsenal player attacking it for a tap-in.

We did find a second though. Gyokeres combined well with Merino around their box, and when he was played through he opened up his body really well and produced a fine finish from close range and a tight angle to make it 2-0. I don’t think that goal at Fleetwood would have done much for his confidence, this felt much more like the kind of strike he needed to produce – for himself as much as the team.

So, we had a good lead at the break, but this was very much a game of two halves. In the first we had 60% possession, out-shot the opposition by 8 to 2, and passed at nearly 90% success rate. In the second, the tables turned. Slavia Prague took 17 shots to our 4, and our pass success fell to 77%. We were sloppy and untidy, they made a tactical change at half-time which worked well for them, and while we weren’t necessarily under the cosh, the entire dynamic of the game changed and we couldn’t get to grips with it.

We needed David Raya to make one superb save to keep them at bay, before Gabriel had to head one off the line, but in injury time they found the goal I think their second half performance (and ours) probably merited. They whipped in a wicked ball from the left, the striker applied the close range finish, and the clean sheet was gone.

Afterwards, Mikel Arteta was happy with the win, but displeased with the second half, saying:

First of all, you have to value the fact it’s very difficult to win away from home. We’ve done it against a very tough opponent, we expected that toughness. In the first half we played at a really high level in terms of intensity, tempo, quality and clarity in what we had to do, and what the game was demanding. We were very efficient – we should have scored three, four or five.

I already talked about some of the things we didn’t do, and others I’d prefer not to mention. It’s a huge lesson, and we’ll learn from the second half. It’s our third away game in quick succession, and we’re the only team to have played three away games in the Champions League and just one at home – there are a lot of factors – but I don’t like to use that, because in the first half we were at the level we wanted. I take full responsibility for the drop in the second half.

I don’t think the team played well at all in the second half, but I do wonder about how we might have done things differently. For example, I feel like Declan Rice played within himself in that second period, and let me be clear, I understand why. Personally, I think it’s a bit mad he did 90+ minutes in a game like this, even if I accept he and the manager know more about his fitness than any of us. Maybe they need him to be like a steam train, going going going all the time, but when you have options of the quality of Myles Lewis-Skelly and Bruno Guimaraes on the bench, surely using them in his stead allows the best of two worlds: some rest for Rice, and fresher legs in midfield when the game is tilting in the opposition’s favour.

We have this really strong bench, but I don’t think the changes we made worked particularly well. The question, of course, is if they absolutely needed to. We had a two goal lead until late on, and we secured all three points away from home after a difficult and physically demanding game at Anfield three days previously. I just found the Jekyll and Hyde nature of of the two halves a little concerning, but only a little. Ten of our sixteen games this season have been away from home, we’ve won seven of them, so that’s a decent return, added to by this victory.

Ultimately, this is essentially a forgettable Champions League tie that we came away with three points from. Apparently it was a year to the day since we played Slavia Prague last season too, a game I had/have zero recollection of. Which might say something about me more than anything else, but these kinds of fixtures don’t live long in the memory. They’re grist for the mill in this part of the season, we had a job to do, and we got it done, and now all the focus turns to Hull on Saturday and the three points required there before the Interlull.

We can talk a bit more about this game in an Arsecast a bit later on this morning, before I head to London a bit later on this afternoon. #1778. Is the Gyokeres iron hot enough for Hull?

I’m here for our book launch which takes place tonight, but also for our game against Hull tomorrow. Mikel Arteta will meet the press this afternoon ahead of that one, and we’ll bring you all the stories on Arseblog News. I don’t think there’s gonna be anything mind-blowing, it looked like we came through the Slavia Prague game without any issues, so fingers crossed that’s the case.

I suppose I’m mildly curious as to whether Viktor Gyokeres’ performance on Wednesday will see him keep his place up front. He got a great goal, provided an assist for Noni Madueke, and probably should have had another assist when he headed back across goal for Mikel Merino, only for the Spaniard to head over the bar when we know he can do better from those situations.

He’s a player who seems to need confidence and rhythm, and on that basis it would make some sense to keep him in the starting line-up. After the last Interlull, when he scored in four successive games for Sweden, I made the case that giving him a start in our first game back would make some sense to try and harness some of what was a good goal scoring run. Strike while the iron is hot and all that.

I looked at a home game against Leeds as the kind of fixture that would suit him. He scored two against them at home last season, and one at Elland Road, but when the time came Mikel Arteta picked Kai Havertz up front. Speaking about the decision to start Gyokeres on Wednesday in Prague, the manager said:

It was a game we believed would be really good for him, for the demands the opponent puts in and the spaces he could use. He’s done it really well, not just for the assist and the goal, but he was really connected to the team. It’s really great news for him, because he really needed that performance.

The question will be does Arteta think Hull at home will be as good for him as Slavia Prague away? After a bright start to the season they haven’t won any of their last seven but they have drawn five of those. Chances are they’re going to come and sit deep, using the blueprint we’ve seen many teams deploy against Arsenal in the past. If a Gyokeres game, if we can call it that, requires the opposition to leave spaces he can use (as per Arteta’s quote above), then maybe this isn’t one of those.

However, on paper, and with all due respect to tomorrow’s opposition, if Hull at home isn’t a Gyokeres game, then it’s hard not to be a bit worried. Personally, I’d be all right to see him start this one, and if it doesn’t work then you have other options. Havertz is the obvious one, but Mikel Merino is an alternative as well with his ability to find spaces inside the opponent’s penalty area. Ideally though, it’s a bit of a building block of a game for the Swedish international. We need him to deliver goals and assists, the last few weeks have been a bit more positive in that regard, and ultimately it’s important that the manager recognises the moments in a season when he might have to choose one player over another for the overall benefit of the team.

Which is to say, I look forward very much to seeing Declan Rice starting up front against Hull tomorrow, and Arteta revealing that his tech-boffins have invented a gizmo which will allow Rice to player 180 minutes in every game. Plus injury time. I kid, obviously, but I suppose we should know by now that regardless of what we think about team selections, use of players, and everything else, this manager will never be even remotely swayed by external noise – and that’s a good thing most of the time!

We will talk a bit more about the Hull game in a quick preview podcast on Patreon a little later on. Because of the book launch, we’ll be recording before the manager meets the press, so bear that in mind.

#1776. Are you ok, Noni?

Arsenal’s squad construction has given them a lot of depth and diversity in terms of profiles. Timber and White for right-back, Calafiori and Hincapie for left-back. Ezri Konsa has, incredibly, offered both protection and threat to the impregnable Saliba and Gabriel partnership. Bruno and Lewis Skelly, Rice and Zubimendi and Odegaard and Merino for midfield.

Eze and Tzolis for the left-wing. Havertz and Gyokeres for centre-forward. Of course, some of these pairings are more symbiotic than others. Mosquera is probably going to fall behind Konsa as a back up to either one of Saliba or Gabriel. In reality, Zubimendi is only going to play ahead of Rice if Rice is injured or Arsenal have a nice easy game against League Two opposition, for example…

On the face of it, Noni Madueke should really be in that third layer of the squad with Mosquera, Kepa and where Zubimendi probably now resides. The role of back-up to Bukayo Saka ought to have been one with limited opportunity. In a sense, I was always a little surprised that Madueke signed up for it when he came to the club from Chelsea last summer.

I was slightly surprised that Arsenal spent so much money on a player who was always incredibly unlikely to dislodge Saka no matter how much he improved. And how much scope was there going to be for Madueke to get the sort of rhythm and consistency of selection to hone his talents?

Now I strongly suspect that Arsenal would have had anxieties over Saka’s ability to stay fit after tearing his hamstring in December 2024 and missing a few months of football. It was the first significant injury Saka had incurred and after quickly deciding that loanee winger Raheem Sterling was not going to be an adequate replacement, they amended for his absence with a blend of 17-year-old Ethan Nwaneri and surplus left-back Kieran Tierney.

It isn’t difficult to see how Arsenal viewed the right-wing spot as a single point of failure but encouraging Madueke to see it as an attractive position must have challenged even Mikel Arteta’s powers of persuasion. Yet just over a year on from signing for Arsenal, Madueke has a league title winners medal (‘while others are tweeting and posting’) with 25 starts to his name last season, 16 of which were in the Premier League.

In reality, being Bukayo Saka’s third leg has, to this point, proved to be a savvy career move for Madueke because he is getting plenty of time on the pitch in Saka’s increasing absences. This extends to the England National Team too, where Madueke plays the same role. But it was a role that still earned him four starts for his country in a World Cup, including a start in the quarter-final against Norway.

A Premier League title winners medal, a Champions League Final appearance and four World Cup starts was not a bad return for Madueke in terms of playing time. I think we knew when Arsenal bought him that Noni was a talented but phlegmatic player, relentless in taking on his full-back but the quality of his end-product could vary markedly.

In his new signing profile of Madueke on Arseblog, Phil Costa wrote, ‘there’s a feeling that Arsenal lack penetration from their wingers (Bukayo Saka aside); chaos factor, some unpredictability, and Madueke brings this in spades. His first thought when receiving the ball is centred around provoking defenders and driving towards goal, which means you can isolate him without too much focus on the overall setup – you just wind him up and let him go.

‘There are two specific metrics to love when assessing the 23-year-old; per FBRef data, he currently sits in the 95th percentile for progressive carries (6.82 per 90) and the 98th percentile for carries into the box (4.12 per 90). Those are big numbers.’ There was never any doubt about Madueke’s ability to get the ball into threatening areas, the question has always been what he does when he gets there.

Last season, some clips of him harumphing the ball out of the stadium on his right foot went semi-viral. I also think some of his performances were impacted by a lack of balance in the front three. With technicians like Havertz and Odegaard unavailable, he was often playing alongside fellow blunderbusses like Gyokeres and Martinelli.

I admit that my tolerance for inefficiency is high when it comes to attackers. I think attacking is a volume game. The vast majority of attacks come to nothing, the vast majority of shots do not go in or even work a goalkeeper. Individual attacks are the weather but, overall, attacking is the climate. The more you do it and sustain it, the more likely you are to score.

So my ‘we can fix him’ gene for slightly wayward wingers is high. I didn’t even mind Gervinho (a frustrating player, no doubt, but the Bradford miss has become the defining image of his Arsenal career which I don’t believe was fully representative of his performances).

The video of Madueke’s right foot ballooning the ball into the upper tier against Kairat last season has been refined. Both his goals this season have been on his right foot, particularly notably against Nottingham Forest where he cut in on his right and unleashed a low and controlled shot. It might have taken a helpful deflection but that’s because he kept the attempt low.

Last season, his right footed efforts were more in danger of colliding with low flying aircraft on their way into orbit. Noni’s goal against Slavia Praha demonstrated his pace in behind. It was the sort of goal and chance Gabriel Martinelli was hoovering up in Europe last season. European games tend to offer more space in behind and with Martinelli gone, Madueke is one of the few Arsenal attackers explosive enough to exploit it.

Indeed, in my view, he ought to have won Arsenal a match winning penalty in Budapest against Paris Saint Germain in May. There are signs of greater maturity and efficiency in his game. According to WhoScored.com his pass success rate in the Premier League last season was 76.2%. This season so far it is 86.3%.

I think he has learned that he does not have to go for the full-back at 100mph every single time he gets the ball and has varied his game. In the Champions League game against Lille, he sent 15 crosses into the penalty area, having sent six into the area in the game before against Leeds. 15 crosses sounds like a lot but it was very clearly under instruction from Mikel Arteta.

After that Lille game, the manager said of Madueke, ‘I said when you talk about players being ‘clinical’, sometimes that means scoring five in every 100. It’s about generating volume, more actions and getting him into the good positions, because he will decide matches. He had a really big contribution a few days ago, today he had a contribution in the last final pass as well.’

Being omitted from the England squad in September, according to Arteta, provided additional motivation for Noni, ‘After the break, he is showing something else, another level of anger, another level of conviction as well as in his actions and he is becoming decisive in matches, which is what we expect from a player like him.’

He has now been omitted from the England squad again for the November international round. It is a decision I don’t really understand from Thomas Tuchel but I am happy if it continues to provide Madueke with an additional reason to fine tune his game and because it hopefully protects a player who has become very important.

I admit I am not entirely sure how good Madueke is going to be in, say, three years’ time. He is 24 and it’s at that age that attackers typically start to increase their decisive actions. He has Max Dowman in the rearview mirror too. I think Madueke has a really high ceiling and there are small, but encouraging, signs of improvement.

#1775. What will happen if Man United get relegated from the Premier League?

By Ben Knapton | 09 Nov 2026 10:04

Setting unwanted record after unwanted record under the beleaguered Michael Carrick, Manchester United - one of the most revered clubs to ever grace the English game - are facing the very real threat of losing their perpetual Premier League status.

Sunday's 4-4 draw with Aston Villa may have seen the Red Devils exhibit their fabulous fightback powers once more, but it also left them celebrating just one win from their first 10 top-flight games of the season, ensuring that they would spend the November international break in the bottom three of the Premier League table.

Only one point separates 18th-placed Man United from rock-bottom Crystal Palace, 16th-placed Nottingham Forest and 17th-placed Coventry City, and the powers-that-be will reportedly hold a meeting to discuss Carrick's future during the domestic hiatus.

A change in management ultimately prevented Tottenham Hotspur from suffering an unthinkable relegation last season, but what if the worst should happen to Man United?

Here, Sports Mole takes a look at what is likely to happen if the Red Devils drop down to the Championship for the 2027-28 season.

It was only a matter of weeks ago that Man United announced record revenues of £677.6m for the 2026 fiscal year, albeit alongside a pre-tax loss of £43m, thanks to their third-placed Premier League finish in 2025-26 and a wave of cost-cutting measures.

However, Man Utd's Championship revenue is estimated to fall to around £375m to £450m, largely thanks to a sharp decline in broadcasting revenues from the loss of Premier League TV deals.

The Red Devils recently recorded £206.8m in broadcasting revenue, but that number is projected to fall to around £55m to £65m in the second tier, and there would also be no European broadcasting boost unless they shock the continent and win the 2026-27 Champions League to qualify for next year's edition.

Man United would also have to reduce ticket prices, potentially bringing their matchday revenue down from just over £150m to just over £100m, although playing 23 home matches rather than 19 - plus the potential of playoffs - would negate that specific impact marginally.

Commercial deals would also suffer a hit, due to expected performance clauses in contracts with kit suppliers and other club sponsors, so a plethora of player sales would be inevitable in order to navigate the massive economical hit as smoothly as possible.

Carrick retains the backing of a large portion of the Man United fanbase, the players are currently receiving mixed receptions, but INEOS and the Glazer family could hardly be held in less esteemed regard.

However, Man Utd fans wondering whether relegation could be the straw that breaks the owners' back are likely to be left disappointed, as the Glazers are not predicted to sell the club even if they drop down to the Championship.

As businessmen, United's owners are supposedly waiting for the perfect moment to cash in on Man Utd, when the club's value is at its highest; in an ideal world, this would be when the Red Devils have moved into their proposed new stadium and are competing in the Champions League, not when they are languishing in the second tier.

INEOS would not survive in its current state, though; sporting director Jason Wilcox and CEO Omar Berrada would almost certainly be moved on, but Ratcliffe could alternatively try to increase his stake in the club while it is at its cheapest; however, that could not happen until 2029.

Interest from the Middle East reportedly remains after Sheikh Jassim's failed takeover bid too, and attempts to wrestle control from Ratcliffe and the Glazers could ramp up as the club's value declines.

Few are expecting Carrick to still be in charge of Man United come 2027, and the current favourites to succeed the Englishman include Mauricio Pochettino, Eddie Howe, Antonio Conte and Julian Nagelsmann.

Roberto De Zerbi affirmed that he would stay at Spurs even if they were relegated last season; the Italian's loyalties were not tested to that extreme, but others' very well could be.

Neither Conte nor Pochettino would be prepared to take on a second-tier project, and the same is almost certainly true of Nagelsmann, although the 39-year-old's youth makes him a slightly more realistic option for a season in the Championship.

Instead, Howe could welcome the opportunity to rebuild the Red Devils, having already guided Bournemouth up the divisions with a limited budget while also taking charge of Burnley for three Championship campaigns.

A viable alternative to Howe is ex-Red Devils assistant and youth manager Kieran McKenna - formerly linked with the United job in 2024 - as the 40-year-old is also unattached, knows the culture of the club and guided Ipswich Town to two Premier League promotions between 2021 and 2026.

Man United players would supposedly not have to worry about any wage cuts in the Championship, as their contracts do not contain specific relegation clauses allowing the Red Devils to slash their salaries.

However, with the next Euros, Copa America and Africa Cup of Nations on the horizon, a mass exodus of big names would be unavoidable, especially with the Red Devils also needing to significantly reduce their operating costs too.

Offloading young players, or those just approaching their prime, would do wonders for the club's financial picture, so Matheus Cunha, Bryan Mbeumo, Benjamin Sesko, Carlos Baleba and Senne Lammens could all be moved on.

Leny Yoro, Kobbie Mainoo and Patrick Dorgu would generate decent sale figures too, but it is not impossible to envisage the young trio sticking around for the rebuild project, if they are willing to accept the potential knock-on effects for Euro 2028 selection.

The club's two highest earners - Bruno Fernandes and Marcus Rashford - would also have to take major pay cuts or depart, and both could therefore be tempted by Saudi Pro League switches despite their deep connection to the Theatre of Dreams.

Fernandes is part of a large group out of contract in 2027 too - a list that also includes Harry Maguire, Tom Heaton, Lisandro Martinez and Luke Shaw - and none should be in line for a renewal if relegation is on the cards.

Joshua Zirkzee, Matthijs de Ligt, Noussair Mazraoui, Manuel Ugarte, Diogo Dalot and Youri Tielemans should all be on the market too, but the same cannot be said for the up-and-coming Carrington prospects.

Expect Ayden Heaven, Shea Lacey, Harry Amass and Jack & Tyler Fletcher to stick around and play central roles in Man United's second-tier season, potentially alongside the returning Chido Obi and Dan Gore, as well as veteran shot-stopper Karl Darlow.

Arsenal are in Premier League action this afternoon, taking on Hull City at home. No doubt there will be some rotation from the midweek Champions League game, with players like Martin Odegaard, Bruno Guimaraes, Myles-Lewis-Skelly, Jurrien Timber, Riccardo Calafiori, Christos Tzolis and Kai Havertz all potential inclusions. I suspect Declan Rice will start!

I wrote yesterday about Viktor Gyokeres and whether his good performance in midweek would see him keep his place. On the Swedish international, Mikel Arteta said:

I think everybody was so happy to see, not only the goals but also the performance, how free he looked, how happy he looked, the energy that he could transmit on that football pitch. That’s exactly what we need, that’s what we’re signing, that’s the type of player that can help us to make the difference and he certainly did that during the night.

So let’s see if that means he keeps his place up front. Noni Madueke has had a decent couple of weeks too, with the manager revealing he’d used the elongated Interlull in October to up the ante in terms of his own training:

What he did is he went abroad and he trained. He got somebody to train him and he went into a programme, he wanted to do that. That’s Noni and that’s his mindset – he wants to get better. I love that action that he took because at that moment he wasn’t playing.

With Bukayo Saka injured and Max Dowman suspended until after the Newcastle game, he’s more or less the only option on the right-hand side, so fingers crossed he can continue that form today against a team who are likely to try and make life difficult for us. Players who can beat a man and find some space are really valuable for fixtures like this, and he might prove very important later on.

Hull started the season brightly, but haven’t won since the end of August. All the same, five draws from their last seven games tells you they’re a relatively tough nut to crack, and with a back five they’ll surely have looked at how other teams have come to our place to frustrate us. An early goal is always useful, Ezri Konsa’s quick strike against Everton probably prevented that game from being as much of a slog as it might have been, but we might also need some patience today too.

Some of the difficult games they’ve come through and competed in, they’ve earned the right to be here and been impressive. We’ve been discussing that with the boys on what to expect from them tomorrow and to be clear on what we need to do to beat them.

#1773. Arsenal 1-0 Hull: Not efficient, but enough

In yesterday’s preview blog, I spoke about Arsenal’s attacking efficiency, and how that might be key to taking all three points. In yesterday’s game against Hull, Arsenal took 21 shots, 10 of which were on target, and scored one goal from that. Efficient?

Despite generally dominating possession, I thought there was a lack of precision in certain aspects of our first half play. Passes weren’t quite quick enough or accurate enough, but there were moments when we could have found the breakthrough. Gabriel almost got on the end of a Noni Madueke cross which was flicked on towards the back post, Rice had a tame shot from a free kick before a late header which he probably should have done better with.

And then there was Kai Havertz. It’s fair to say Hull didn’t leave a lot of room behind a defensive line that often had six players stretched across it, but late in the half a superb Martin Odegaard pass sent him clean through, one on one with the keeper. I haven’t seen replays but in real time I felt like he should have pulled the trigger – instead he over-complicated it. You have to be prepared to shoot from there, even if it’s on your wrong foot.

Then there was a penalty incident when he complained vociferously, play went on, the ref was then told to go to the screen and we all assumed it would be a penalty. However, the ref said it was a foul but Havertz was offside – and it felt like a massive waste of time. Afterwards, it emerged it should have been a penalty, but apparently the rule is ‘open to interpretation’. So clear as mud then.

In the second half, we seemed to play down our right a lot, with Madueke the outlet most of the time. I thought he did pretty well, much better than Christos Tzolis on the other side, but the breakthrough wouldn’t come. Mikel Merino replaced Rice (who seemed to be on the end of a wild challenge in midfield that the ref just ignored as he tumbled through the air), and Viktor Gyokeres came on for Havertz.

On 71 minutes though, we found the goal. Madueke’s shot was spilled by the keeper, Odegaard was quickest to react to poke the ball home for 1-0. And to be fair, you always felt confident that would be enough. We are the masters of the single goal margin win, and this was another one. Not a day that will live long in the memory or anything, but a 1-0 win that takes us into the Interlull in really good shape, and there’s not much arguing with that.

Or really, much more to say about this game. Mikel Arteta sounded happy enough, saying:

I’m delighted with the win. To go into the international break with a win is one of the best things about being a coach or player, I would say. Regarding the performance, I thought we were the better team, had enough chances to score and make it bigger for ourselves and we weren’t efficient enough to take them.

We then had to rely on generating volume, plenty of persisting until we finally broke them down. Martin then got the goal. Not the most beautiful one, but the most effective one, a simple ‘shoot and then follow the next action’, and that was ultimately enough to win the game.

So Arsenal sit top of the table, with 9 wins from 10 so far this season in the league, and it’s a very impressive run of form. Do I wish we had more attacking potency? Absolutely, and I do worry a bit that it might bite us in the arse somewhere down the line, but for now, we can see that this is a team that just knows how to win, and perhaps that’s the most important thing.

Right, I’m gonna leave it there for this morning. I have to head back to Dublin today. It was great to see lots of you over the weekend, until next time! And we’ll have an Arsecast Extra for you tomorrow too.

#1771. Strops, scruff, and chaos

I watched Man Utd v Aston Villa last night. When Villa conceded late on to let a two goal lead slip for the second time in the game, Unai Emery threw a strop and went down the tunnel. It’s not the first time he’s eschewed a handshake with the opposition manager, and his post-game interview where he insisted he thought the game was over was very funny because it was such obvious bullshit.

This is someone who has managed over 1000 games in his career. I’m pretty sure he knows when the final whistle blows and when it doesn’t. Can you imagine if Mikel Arteta did that? You wouldn’t be able to move for all the opinion pieces about what a sore loser he is and all the rest. But perhaps Emery gets a pass because he is ‘the best manager in the league’. Anyway, perhaps it provides a stay of execution for Michael Carrick at Man Utd, which can only be a good thing.

Meanwhile, it looks as if Pierre Sage is gonna get fired by Crystal Palace and replaced by Thomas Frank. That seems a sensible appointment to me. Enough time has passed since his spell at Sp*rs for the toxins to wear off, and he’s clearly a good manager. I’ve never been convinced by Sage, I just think he looks too scruffy. As if someone got a 10 year old to draw man and brought it to life.

I quite enjoyed this quote from Mikel Arteta in his post-game press conference after Saturday’s 1-0 win over Hull:

Sometimes we try to score the perfect goal against low blocks, but we need to be much more chaotic than that. If we open the scoring much earlier also, it changes the game.

I love it as a concept, adding some chaos to our control makes a lot of sense, but it also kinda seems at odds with what the manager asks of his players. Maybe he just means more shots from distance, maybe riskier pass when we’re trying to break the opposition down, or maybe there’s something he’s got cooking for over the Interlull and when we return we see something we never expected. He did kick the shit out of a dugout chair on Saturday, that’s a new enough development to be fair.

I wonder was he referring to the Kai Havertz chance in the first half, when he could have shot on his right foot but tried to cut back/lay it off. If you shoot, maybe you don’t score but as we saw with the winning goal from Martin Odegaard, it might end up in the path of another Arsenal player who can finish it off. Perhaps too there’s a bit of a through line between being more chaotic and what Noni Madueke is doing at the moment. He can be a bit scattergun, but as Nick Wright points out on Sky Sports, his numbers are improving. I don’t think Arteta will ever embrace full chaos, all the time, but if he can add a little more to the mix, it could certainly help.

Right, I have to leave it there for this morning. A bit shorter than normal, I know. We will have an Arsecast Extra for you a bit later on though. #1770. Chelsea transfer news: Blues outcast 'targeted' by Roma after Gian Piero Gasperini request

By Darren Plant | 09 Nov 2026 10:26

Chelsea winger Jamie Gittens has reportedly remained as a serious transfer target for Roma.

During the summer window, the former Borussia Dortmund attacker emerged as a potential signing for the Italian giants, who had secured a return to the Champions League.

Like in the summer, Roma would prefer to negotiate a loan deal for Gittens, rather than pay a substantial fee for his signature.

Since picking up a serious hamstring injury at the end of January, Gittens has not made a single appearance in the Premier League.

Even when he returns to fitness, there is little prospect of him earning regular starts under Alonso, particularly when Chelsea are only playing Premier League games until January.

The aim now should be trying to protect his £50m+ transfer fee by allowing him to go elsewhere and play games, wherever that may be.

With teams prepared to pay a loan fee for his signature, it should be an easy exit to facilitate.
